additions.reason: The teaching opens with this phrase as its entire topic: 'דְּמוּת דְּיוֹקְנוֹ שֶׁל אָבִיו רָאָה' — he [Yosef] saw the image/form of his father. The Rebbe then immediately declares: 'הוּא דָּבָר נִסְתָּר מְאֹד' — IT (the דמות דיוקן) IS a very hidden matter. This IS-statement is the teaching's first and most fundamental identification: the phenomenon of the paternal image appearing IS its essential quality of hiddenness. The word 'הוּא' here functions as a bechina marker — the image IS (=belongs to the domain of) the hidden. The concept is central to the talmudic aggadah (Sotah 36b): at the moment of temptation by Potiphar's wife, Yosef saw the image of his father Yaakov appearing in a window/aperture, and this vision caused him to resist. The Rebbe's entire teaching is a reflection on the nature of this concept. 'דמות דיוקנו של אביו' as a node represents the protective ancestral/paternal image — a concept that appears in multiple Rebbe Nachman teachings about spiritual lineage and protection. Proposed bechina edges: (a) דמות דיוקנו של אביו ↔ דבר נסתר מאד — the image IS a hidden matter by nature; (b) דמות דיוקנו של אביו ↔ מעלת הנסיון — the image's appearance IS what constitutes the greatness of the trial.

additions.reason: The Rebbe uses the word 'מַעֲלַת הַנִּסָּיוֹן' — the excellence or greatness of the trial. This phrase introduces a bechina-type claim: the trial (נִסָּיוֹן) has a specific quality (מַעֲלָה), and that quality IS the fact that these are hidden and concealed matters. The concept of נִסָּיוֹן in this teaching belongs to the positive/good domain: Yosef's trial was one he passed, and the Rebbe is meditating on the positive dimension — the spiritual height of undergoing such a test, the fact that the protective mechanism (the image of the father) operates through channels that are beyond human understanding. נִסָּיוֹן here is not the temptation itself (which would be neutral or evil-adjacent) but rather the spiritual challenge and its associated miraculous dimension. Polarity is good because the entire framing is laudatory: the Rebbe is speaking about the greatness of what happened to Yosef, not about the danger or the yetzer hara's role.

additions.reason: The phrase 'דְּבָרִים נִסְתָּרִים וּמְכֻסִּים מִבְּנֵי אָדָם' (hidden and concealed matters from people) is the teaching's conclusion and its defining characterization of the entire phenomenon discussed. The Rebbe uses this phrase as the summative quality of both the image-mechanism (how the image appears) and the trial's greatness. The phrase appears at the climax of the two-sentence teaching — it IS the theological category to which the Rebbe assigns this entire discussion. 'Hidden and concealed from people' in Rebbe Nachman's system is a positive category — it belongs to the domain of nistar (esoteric, divine mystery), which is the dimension of spiritual reality beyond human rational grasp. This is opposed to the public, graspable domain — but not opposed in a good/evil sense. Rather, it represents the deepest level of positive divine action: the hidden dimension of divine providence and spiritual protection. This node is likely new to the dataset in this formulation (the paired phrase 'נסתרים ומכוסים' as a compound concept is distinctive). It is the dominant qualifier that unifies the other two nodes.

concepts_examined_and_excluded.reason: Yaakov is mentioned as the subject whose image appeared to Yosef ('דְּמוּת דְּיוֹקְנוֹ שֶׁל אָבִיו' = the image of Yaakov, his father). The text says 'בְּוַדַּאי יַעֲקֹב לֹא יָדַע' — Yaakov certainly did not know [that his image appeared]. Yaakov is cited as an actor/subject in the narrative, not as a concept being identified via bechina language. The teaching does not say 'Yaakov IS a bechina of X.' He is the source of the image, but the Rebbe does not make a bechina equation involving Yaakov himself in this Torah. Excluded as not a bechina node for this reference, though Yaakov is a major node in many other Torahs (especially Torah #1 where Yaakov IS a bechina of the one who attaches to sekhel).

Yosef is the subject of the talmudic aggadah — it was he who saw the image (the implicit subject of 'רָאָה' in the lemma, and 'הוּא בְּעַצְמוֹ אֵינוֹ יוֹדֵעַ' refers to Yosef). However, the Rebbe does not use bechina language to identify Yosef with any other concept in this teaching. He is the protagonist of the narrative but not a node in a bechina equation within this Torah. Yosef is a major bechina node in many other Torahs (as a bechina of tzaddik, yesod, etc.) but not in this specific teaching, which is a reflection on the mechanism and nature of the miracle rather than on Yosef's spiritual archetype.

concepts_examined_and_excluded.reason: The teaching twice emphasizes not-knowing: Yosef himself does not know how the image appeared, and certainly Yaakov did not know. This is a repeated emphasis — 'הוּא בְּעַצְמוֹ אֵינוֹ יוֹדֵעַ... יַעֲקֹב לֹא יָדַע.' The not-knowing is a consequence/aspect of the hiddenness, not a separate concept being identified as a bechina. The Rebbe is explaining what 'hidden and concealed from people' means — it means even the people directly involved in the miracle do not know its mechanism. 'לא ידע' is descriptive content of the 'דברים נסתרים ומכוסים' category, not an independent bechina node. Excluded as a sub-aspect of 'דברים נסתרים ומכוסים' rather than a separate node.

The word 'מַעֲלַת הַנִּסָּיוֹן' (the quality/excellence of the trial) introduces the bechina identification. However, 'מַעֲלָה' itself is a grammatical construct here (smichut) — it means 'the quality belonging to the trial,' not a standalone concept named 'מַעֲלָה.' It is the connector that declares the nisayon's quality, not a separate bechina node. The actual concept being identified IS 'דברים נסתרים ומכוסים' — the hiddenness. 'מעלה' is the bridge-word of the identification, like how 'הוא בחינת' or 'נקרא' are bridge words in standard bechina formulations.

The temptation (the potential evil pole) is not named or developed. The teaching's entire content is an appreciation of the hidden positive mechanism that enabled Yosef's spiritual protection. This is structurally different from most Rebbe Nachman teachings that develop explicit good/evil pairs — Torah #150 is a meditative observation, not a structural teaching with opposing poles.
